title: Bhrigu and the riddle of Brahman
hookLine: Varuna won't define Brahman; he sends his son Bhrigu to look again until he sees it.
carry: brahman is pointed to, then seen for yourself
tomorrow: a fortune on the table, and a wife who asks for something more.
last: THE FIRST LINE IS A HUNGER.

cards: Ask a good math teacher for the answer, and she slides the problem back across the desk. Try it again. Bhrigu gets the same treatment, and he's asking about everything.
He walks up to his father, Varuna. Sir, teach me Brahman. His father doesn't define it.
He gives a riddle. That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they go back: try to know that. That is Brahman.
So Bhrigu goes off and practices austerity, and he comes back sure he has it. Brahman is food. His father sends him away again.

teach.h: THE SOURCE, SUPPORT AND RESTING PLACE.
teach.b: That story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad, and Shankara reads the second sutra through it. The sutra is short: janmady asya yatah. In paraphrase: that from which the birth and the rest of this world come.

The rest, Shankara explains, means its staying in being and its coming to an end. So Brahman is pointed out the way Varuna pointed it out: as the source, the support and the resting place of everything.
Notice it's pointing, not picturing. The sutra doesn't say what Brahman looks like. It says where to look.
Isn't this just an argument, reasoning from a world to its cause? No, he says. The sutra gathers the Upanishad's own words.

Reasoning helps when it agrees with them, but the knowing rests on the texts, and finally on direct realization. Which is why Varuna won't just say it. A pointed-to thing has to be seen by the one looking.
Bhrigu goes again, and comes back with breath. Then mind. Then understanding.
Each time, again. At last he sees Brahman as bliss, ananda. This is one of Hinduism's deepest teachings about God.
Brahman, the one reality everything is born from, lives by and goes back to, can't be handed over as a definition. A teacher can only point. The seeing has to happen in you.
That's jnana: return after return, each answer peeled back until the source shows itself.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, the Bhrigu story is often taught alongside the second sutra, and some teachers guide students to look past body, breath and mind toward the self that knows them.

o: knowledge reached by looking again and again
a proof of God built from logic alone
an answer a teacher hands over at the door

games.q: the second sutra and Bhrigu's search. tap the pairs.
p: that from which this world comes
the father who gives a riddle

s: the second sutra proves Brahman by pure logic, from the world to its cause
Shankara says it gathers the Upanishad's words; reasoning helps, but the knowing rests on the texts and realization.
the sutra describes what Brahman looks like
it points: the source, support and resting place of everything. it says where to look.
Bhrigu is sent back again after each answer until he sees Brahman as bliss
food, breath, mind, understanding, then bliss.

games.q: you're Varuna. your son has come back sure that Brahman is food. what do you do?
o: tell him the right answer, to save time.
praise him; food is the final answer.
games.why: Varuna sends him back each time: food, breath, mind, understanding, until Bhrigu sees Brahman as bliss. A pointed-to thing has to be seen by the one looking.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back. On the way out, notice your feet; on the way back, notice the breath; then sit, and notice what has been noticing all along.
If walking isn't easy right now, make the same trip with your attention, from feet to breath to the one who's aware.

wordCard.voice: Jnana: knowledge that frees. In Bhrigu's story, it's reached by looking again and again, each answer peeled back.

orig.note: Sanskrit ananda, bliss; where Bhrigu's search arrives in the Taittiriya Upanishad.

carryVoice: Keep this one, Varuna's way: Brahman is pointed to, then seen for yourself. See you tomorrow.
